summary: In networks where endpoints can see or choose among paths, they need a shared way to describe path characteristics. This informational document defines and categorizes path properties and identifies several that may help endpoints select paths or invoke services. It comes from the Path Aware Networking Research Group.

eli5.summary: When picking a road trip route, you'd like words for things like how fast, how bumpy, or how safe a road is. This lists useful words for describing network roads.

questions: what is a path property in networking
how can path properties help applications
subtitle: A shared vocabulary for describing network paths and their characteristics

tldr.problem: Networks and endpoints currently lack a common language to describe what paths are available, what their characteristics are, and what services they provide, making it impossible for applications to choose intelligently among paths or for networks to signal capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines path elements (nodes and links), paths, and path properties—measurable or observable traits like delay, loss, capacity, and transparency—and provides examples of properties useful for path selection, protocol choice, and service invocation.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints and networks can now use consistent terminology to reason about paths, enabling path-aware networking where applications adapt to network conditions rather than the network adapting to applications.

facts.label: Key vocabulary items
facts.value: Path, node, link, flow, property, observed, assessed, target

today: RFC 9473 is an Informational document from the IRTF Path Aware Networking Research Group. It provides the foundational vocabulary for path-aware networking but does not itself specify mechanisms for discovering or advertising path properties. Future standards can build on these definitions to enable path-aware applications and networks.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
The current Internet routes packets based on destination IP address, but endpoints and applications have no standard way to discover what paths are available, what their properties are, or how they differ from one another. This is the gap that path-aware networking aims to fill. Rather than the network forcing a single path and the application adapting to whatever performance results, path-aware networking lets endpoints discover and reason about paths, and adapt their behavior accordingly.

To enable this, everyone needs a shared vocabulary. This RFC provides that vocabulary. It defines what a path is, what path elements (nodes and links) compose it, and what properties can be observed or measured about paths. The document does not assume any property is actually available to endpoints; it only defines the concepts so that future specifications can build on them consistently.
sections.eli5: Delivery companies and packages need a common language to talk about roads: short, expensive, private, fast, bumpy, safe. This document defines those words.

sections.title: Core Definitions
sections.content:
A path is a sequence of path elements (nodes and links) that packets traverse from a source to a destination. Paths are unidirectional and time-dependent; the path a packet takes can change at any moment. A node is an on-path entity that processes packets (routers, switches, firewalls, even a single queue). A link is a communication facility between two nodes.

An endpoint is the start or end node of a path (typically a host). A flow is one or more packets that share traits with respect to a path. A property is a measurable trait of a path element or a flow with respect to a path (e.g., delay, loss rate, administrative domain). Properties can be observed (measured on actual packets), assessed (predicted or calculated), or target properties (goals set by an endpoint).

Importantly, path representations can differ based on the observer's visibility or level of abstraction. An endpoint might see paths as sequences of routers, while a different context might represent paths as sequences of autonomous systems.
sections.eli5: A path is the road. Nodes are intersections and houses. A link is one street segment. A flow is a specific delivery. A property is something you can measure about the road, like its width.

sections.title: What You Can Do With Path Properties
sections.content:
Path properties enable three main use cases. Path selection allows endpoints or networks to choose among available paths based on properties like delay, capacity, cost, or policy constraints. An endpoint with two wireless interfaces might prefer the lower-latency path for interactive applications and the higher-capacity path for file transfers. A network might use path properties in BGP decisions instead of a single MED value.

Protocol selection means choosing a transport protocol or configuring protocol parameters based on path properties. An application might try QUIC on paths that support it, fall back to TCP elsewhere, or choose video quality based on observed link capacity. Service invocation allows endpoints to activate service functions (firewalls, transcoding, etc.) on particular paths to achieve specific goals, such as privacy or performance enhancement.
sections.eli5: If the road is bumpy, use a truck with good suspension. If it's expensive, send a smaller package. If you need privacy, take the private road.

sections.title: Examples of Path Properties
sections.content:
The RFC lists numerous path properties organized into categories. Administrative properties include the identity of who controls a node (ASN, domain, operator) and the routing domain identifier. Topology properties include disjointness (how many shared elements two paths have) and whether paths are symmetric (reverse paths use the same elements in reverse order).

Transparency properties describe whether a node cares about packet contents: a transparent firewall does not modify packets; a non-transparent NAT actively changes them. Performance properties include link capacity, link usage, one-way delay, delay variation, and packet loss. These can be observed, assessed, or measured in aggregate. Service properties include what protocols are available (QUIC, MPTCP), what features work (ECN, TCP Fast Open), and what service functions are present (NAT, transcoding). Resource properties include monetary cost and access technology (Wi-Fi, cellular, wired).

A key distinction is between dynamic properties (delay, loss, which change moment to moment) and non-dynamic properties (MTU, administrative domain, which rarely change). Consumers of dynamic properties must be careful to avoid oscillation caused by stale measurements.
sections.eli5: You can describe a road by: who owns it, whether it connects to other roads, if there are toll booths, how fast you can go, how bumpy it is, whether trucks are allowed, or whether it's paved.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Path-aware applications that trust path properties need assurance that the properties are accurate. If an endpoint makes policy or routing decisions based on path properties, it must be able to verify them (e.g., through cryptographic proof or a trusted intermediary). Revealing target path properties to the network can leak user privacy: if an endpoint says 'I want low-latency paths', a network operator can infer something about the application or user behavior.

Privacy-enhancing technologies like MASQUE proxies may obscure paths, reducing visibility and thus the usefulness of path-aware mechanisms. The document notes that security and trust properties (confidentiality, integrity) are orthogonal to path properties themselves, since they apply to the communicating parties and their keys rather than to what the network does to packets. Defining such properties is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If you tell someone 'I need a fast route', they know you're in a hurry. A relay service can hide that you're going somewhere at all, but then the relay has to know the secret.
